newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian prime minister on verge of falling.
newsitem.headline: Indian prime minister on verge of falling.

text.p: Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda faced almost certain defeat in a confidence vote in parliament on Friday after last-ditch talks with its former ally, the Congress party, collapsed.
Deve Gowda's defeat could pave the way for the second general election in a year or a period of political uncertainty as parties struggle to patch together a new majority in the hung parliament.

The political crisis has held the business-friendly 1997/98 (April-March) budget hostage and unsettled financial markets. The Bombay bourse's key index was down more than 1.5 percent in early trade on Friday.
The prime minister's fate appeared sealed when negotiations between his 15-party United Front coalition and Congress ended in deadlock on Thursday.
The United Front refused to buckle under Congress pressure to abandon Deve Gowda, who was propelled into power last June after inconclusive general elections.
Congress, hoping for a split in the centre-left governing coalition that would allow it to claim power, stood by its demand that Deve Gowda resign.

Waiting in the wings was the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), which led the nation for 12 days last year and would like to go to the polls again to strengthen its chances of recapturing power.

The 542-member lower house of parliament, the Lok Sabha, was set to convene in a special session at 11 a.m. (0530 GMT) to begin debate on a one-line motion: "That this House expresses its confidence in the Council of Ministers."
The speaker, P.A. Sangma, had scheduled eight hours of debate, and a vote was expected after 8 p.m. (1430 GMT).

Deve Gowda would need a simple majority of members present and voting to survive, but the arithmetic appeared stacked against him. "Breakdown: Gowda Will Go," said a headline in The Asian Age, which called the political crisis "collective suicide".
His alliance of regional, leftwing and centrist parties controls 178 votes, according to updated parliament figures.
Congress, which sparked the 13-day crisis by unexpectedly withdrawing its vital support to Deve Gowda, on Thursday ordered its 140 deputies to vote against the motion.
The BJP and its four allies, with 193 votes, decided on Friday to vote against Deve Gowda.
Failing a miracle deal between the United Front and Congress or a decision by Deve Gowda to resign, the prime minister was expected to lose the test vote.
His defeat could lead to a myriad of scenarios.

Constitutional experts said Deve Gowda could ask President Shankar Dayal Sharma to dissolve the lower house of parliament and call snap elections, but the president would not be obliged to accept the recommendation.
The president could turn to the BJP as the biggest group in parliament. But the president could also tap a leader of another party if he felt that person could muster a majority.
Congress appeared to be banking on the possibility that, after the vote, the United Front would be prepared to negotiate a power-sharing deal without Deve Gowda at the helm.

Speculation on a possible compromise choice earlier this week centred on G.K. Moopanar, a former Congress member from the southern state of Tamil Nadu who broke away last year to form the Tamil Maanila Congress, part of the United Front.
Moopanar met the president late on Thursday, fanning more speculation.
The fate of the budget, which would slash taxes and had spurred a rally in stock prices after being unveiled on February 28, was uncertain.
House Speaker P.A. Sangma met the president on Thursday to express concern that some key provisions of the budget would lapse if parliament failed to pass it by May 14.
Sangma told the president the country would face a constitutional crisis if the Lok Sabha was dissolved without passage of the budget.
